definitionControls.title: Coordinate monument and coordinate survey system definitions
definitionControls.mainQuestion: What do coordinate monument and coordinate survey system mean in the Surveys Act?
guidedQuestions: What is a coordinate monument under the Surveys Act?
What is a coordinate survey system under the Surveys Act?
answers: A coordinate monument is a brass, bronze, or aluminum cap or plate established and maintained in accordance with section 3.
A coordinate survey system is a system established under section 2.

definitionControls.title: Corner and legal monument definitions
definitionControls.mainQuestion: How does the Surveys Act define a corner and a legal monument?
guidedQuestions: What is a corner under the Surveys Act?
What is a legal monument under the Surveys Act?
answers: A corner is a point in an intersection of boundaries of land.
A legal monument is a device planted by a surveyor.

definitionControls.title: Survey and surveyor definitions
definitionControls.mainQuestion: What do survey and surveyor mean in the Surveys Act?
guidedQuestions: What is a survey under the Surveys Act?
Who is a surveyor under the Surveys Act?
answers: A survey is a survey to define the boundaries of land.
A surveyor is a New Brunswick Land Surveyor.

definitionControls.title: Regulator assistance to the Board
definitionControls.mainQuestion: When may a regulator assist the Energy and Utilities Board, and what information may the Board receive?
guidedQuestions: What does regulator mean for section 49.1 of the Energy and Utilities Board Act?
What must have happened before a non-party regulator may assist the Board under subsection 49.1(2)?
What information may the Board receive and accept from an assisting regulator?
answers: For section 49.1, “regulator” means a regulator as defined in the Financial and Consumer Services Commission Act.

The Board must apply following the commencement of a proceeding resulting from the application of financial and consumer services legislation, and the regulator must not already be a party to the proceedings.
The Board may receive and accept information from the regulator that it considers relevant, whether or not the information would be admissible in a court of law.

v3Controls.approvedGroup: Instrument record, examination, acceptance, and rejection

v3.mainQuestion: How does the registrar process an instrument from receipt through acceptance or rejection under section 18?
guidedQuestions: What must the registrar assign and record when an instrument is received?
What happens after the instrument is recorded for examination?
On what grounds may the registrar refuse to file or register and reject an instrument?
studyAnswers: The registrar shall assign a registration number, date, and time to every instrument received at the land titles office for filing or registration, and shall enter the instrument, date, time, and number in the instrument record.

The instrument is examined and, subject to subsection 18(4), a record of its acceptance for filing or registration is entered in the instrument record. When accepted for registration under subsection 18(2), it shall be registered.

The registrar may reject an instrument if the appropriate fee has not been paid, if it does not relate to land in the district, lacks the approved parcel identifier or is otherwise incomplete, uses a retired parcel identifier or an added description, is not in proper form or fit for filing or registration, or does not comply with the Community Planning Act if applicable.

What does 18(4) require or allow for Instrument record, examination, acceptance, and rejection?

The instrument shall then be examined and, subject to subsection (4), a record of the acceptance of the instrument for filing or registration shall be entered in the instrument record.
When an instrument is accepted for registration pursuant to subsection (2), it shall be registered.

Notwithstanding anything in this or any other enactment, the registrar may refuse to file or register and may reject an instrument where the appropriate fee has not been paid therefor or where the instrument (a) does not relate to land situated in his district; (b) does not describe the land to which it relates by its approved parcel identifier, or is otherwise incomplete; (b.1) describes the land (i) by reference...

remediatedV4.mainQuestion: What steps does the registrar follow when an instrument is received, examined, accepted, or rejected for filing or registration?

What happens after an instrument is recorded as received and then accepted for registration?
On what grounds may the registrar refuse to file or register, and may reject, an instrument?
studyAnswers: The registrar shall assign a registration number, date, and time to every instrument received and enter a record of the instrument, date, time, and number in the instrument record.

The instrument is examined and, subject to the rejection power in subsection 18(4), a record of acceptance for filing or registration is entered in the instrument record; when accepted for registration, it shall be registered.

The registrar may refuse to file or register and may reject an instrument if the appropriate fee has not been paid, or if the instrument does not relate to land in the registrar's district, lacks the approved parcel identifier or is otherwise incomplete, uses a retired parcel identifier or adds a description in addition to the approved parcel identifier, is not in proper form or fit for filing or registration, or does not comply with the Community Planning Act if applicable.

v3Controls.approvedGroup: Rejection notice, amending instruments, and discretionary Registry Act document registration

v3.mainQuestion: What rules govern rejection records, amending instruments, and discretionary registration of Registry Act documents under section 18?
guidedQuestions: What must the registrar do when an instrument is rejected?
What instrument shall the registrar not reject despite subsection 18(4)?
How may an instrument filed or registered under the Act be amended?
When may a Registry Act document dealing with registered land be registered under the Land Titles Act?
studyAnswers: The registrar shall enter in the instrument record a record of the rejection and a memorandum of the reasons, and shall notify the person who presented the instrument for registration.
Notwithstanding subsection 18(4), the registrar shall not reject an instrument referred to in subsection 12(10).
An instrument filed or registered under the Act may, subject to terms and conditions imposed by the registrar, be amended by filing or registering an amending instrument in prescribed form.

If a document sufficient to pass an estate or interest in land under the Registry Act deals with land registered under the Land Titles Act, the Registrar General may, in absolute discretion, order the proper registrar to register it under the Land Titles Act; once registered, it has the same effect as if registered as an instrument.

v3Controls.approvedGroup: Subdivision public-purpose land, money, procedure, summary, and filing rules

v3.mainQuestion: What public-purpose land, money, procedure, summary, and filing rules may subdivision regulations address under section 125?
guidedQuestions: What may a subdivision regulation provide for under subsection 125(10)?
What modified rules apply if a subdivision regulation under section 125 is in effect?
How must public-purpose land and money in lieu be held or used?
What must the Minister do before making a regulation under section 125?
What do subsections 125(15) and 125(16) say about summaries and filing?
studyAnswers: It may provide for setting aside public-purpose land or paying money in lieu at the Minister discretion, vest specified access and subdivision-plan approval powers in a regional service commission, prescribe tentative-plan approval fees, make subdivision street naming subject to regional service commission approval, and add exemptions under subsection 80(1).

Section 77 applies with necessary modifications, except that a plan setting aside public-purpose land cannot be approved unless the regional service commission recommends the location and the Minister approves and signs the plan; variance powers under section 78 are vested in the regional service commission or development officer, and sections 79 and 80 apply with necessary modifications.

Land vested in the Crown shall be held undeveloped or developed for public purposes and may later be conveyed to a local government if included within its boundaries. Money received in lieu of land or from sale of the land must go into a special account and be spent only to acquire or develop public-purpose land, with investment earnings paid into that account and later local-government transfer rules if applicable.

Before making a regulation, the Minister shall request views from the regional service commission if the regulation would have effect in a region, request advisory committee views for specified rural district regulations, and follow, with necessary modifications, the preliminary by-law procedure under section 111 except for regulations under paragraph 125(1)(a), (b), (f), or (g).

For a zoning regulation or rural plan, section 111 does not require the Minister to make the proposed rural plan or amendment available for public consideration if a written summary is made available. The Director shall file a copy of each regulation in the land registration office for every affected county, but filing is not a condition precedent to the regulation coming into force.

remediatedV4.mainQuestion: What public-purpose, procedural, summary, and filing rules apply to subdivision and other regulations under section 125?
guidedQuestions: What matters may a subdivision regulation under section 125 address?
What procedural rules apply when a subdivision regulation under section 125 is in effect?
How must public-purpose land and money in lieu of that land be handled under section 125?
What must the Minister do before making a regulation under section 125, and what written-summary exception applies?
Where must the Director file section 125 regulations, and is filing a condition for them to come into force?
studyAnswers: A subdivision regulation may provide for setting aside public-purpose land, money in lieu of that land at the Minister discretion, regional service commission powers over access and subdivision-plan approval, tentative-plan approval fees, regional service commission approval of subdivision street names, and added exemptions for land in the regulation area.

Section 77 applies with necessary modifications, except that a plan involving public-purpose land shall not be approved unless the regional service commission has recommended the land location and the Minister has approved and signed the plan. Section 78 variance powers are vested in the regional service commission or development officer, and sections 79 and 80 apply with necessary modifications.

Land vested in the Crown shall be held undeveloped or developed for public purposes, may later be conveyed to a local government if included within its boundaries, and is subject to the Act provisions affecting public-purpose land vested in a local government. Money received in lieu of land or from sale of land goes to a special account and may be spent only to acquire or develop land for public purposes, with investment earnings added and remaining amounts paid to a later-included local government as stated.

Before making a section 125 regulation, the Minister shall request regional service commission views if the regulation would affect a region, request advisory committee views for a section 51 regulation affecting a rural district with an advisory committee, and follow the section 111 preliminary by-law procedure with necessary modifications, except for regulations under paragraph 125(1)(a), (b), (f), or (g). For a zoning regulation under subsection 125(1) or a rural plan under section 51, section 111 does not require making the proposed rural plan or amendment available for public consideration if the Minister makes a written summary available.

The Director shall file a copy of each section 125 regulation in the land registration office for every county where affected land is situated, but filing is not a condition precedent to the regulation coming into force.

v3.mainQuestion: How must an objection to boundary confirmation be submitted, and when does it require a hearing?
guidedQuestions: By what methods and by when must an objection be delivered?
What must the written statement of objection set out?
When must the Registrar General hold a hearing after an objection?
studyAnswers: The objector shall deliver the objection to the Registrar General by personal service, registered mail, or courier service before the deadline stipulated in the notice sent under subsection 9(1) or (2).
It must set out the reasons for the objection and any grounds and arguments in relation to the objection.

If a written statement of objection is delivered before the deadline in accordance with subsection 10(1), the Registrar General shall hold a hearing to determine the validity of the objection and, if applicable, the validity of the applicant claim that the boundaries lie as shown on the plan of survey.

studyAnswers: The options apply if no written statement of objection is delivered before the deadline in accordance with subsection 10(1).

If not satisfied by all material filed in the proceeding, including the application if applicable, that the boundary or boundaries should be confirmed, the Registrar General may hold a hearing in accordance with the Act and regulations.

v3Controls.approvedGroup: Lease, official-sale, sheriff-sale, and will registration timing exceptions

v3.mainQuestion: What registration timing exceptions protect certain leases, sale conveyances, and wills under section 19?
guidedQuestions: Which leases need not be registered merely to avoid being fraudulent and void?
When is an official-capacity public-auction conveyance protected as if registered at the time of sale?
When is a sheriff sale conveyance protected as if registered on its execution day?
When is a registered will protected as if registered immediately after death?
studyAnswers: A lease for a term not exceeding three years need not be registered, and is not deemed fraudulent and void merely for non-registration, if actual possession goes along with the lease; this does not apply to leases over three years or leases without actual possession.

When a person in an official capacity executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold at public auction pursuant to law, the conveyance is as valid against subsequent purchasers or judgment creditors as if registered at the time of sale if registered within six months of the day of sale.

If a sheriff executes a conveyance of an interest in lands sold under the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act, it is as valid against subsequent purchasers or judgment creditors as if registered on the day of execution if registered within six months after the day of execution.

A will is as valid against subsequent purchasers or judgment creditors as if registered immediately after death if registered within six months after death when the testator died in the Province, or within one year after death when the testator died outside the Province.

v3.mainQuestion: What affidavit must accompany a deed transferring real property, and what must the registrar do with it?
